https://www.dw.com/en/uk-village-votes-t.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MiSw Residents of Piddington near Oxford celebrated the symbolic vote result on Wednesday Image: Joe Giddens/PA Images/picture alliance Advertisement An English village of about 350 people has voted to "secede" from the United Kingdom , in a symbolic protest against government plans to set up an asylum reception center nearby. Residents of Piddington, about 25 kilometers (15 miles) northeast of Oxford, celebrated with a placard reading "Principality of Piddington" near the village road sign on Wednesday. They oppose plans, still under review, to house asylum seekers in a disused military base, MoD Bicester (Site A). Piddington is home to about 350 people and has few amenities or facilities to speak of Image: Joe Giddens/PA Images/picture alliance What happened in the tongue-in-cheek breakaway vote? The village's parish council said that 312 people cast ballots in the vote, a turnout of almost 92%. Participants in the vote, which had no legal basis, were asked to agree or disagree with the statement: "I support Piddington seeking to secede from the United Kingdom and pursuing self-determination." Of them, 285 voted to secede, 26 voted against, and one spoiled their ballot. Parish council chair Tim McNally said that, going forward, the village would identify as the "Principality of Piddington." "For us, it's about proportiality," McNally told Sky News. "How does a small village of 350 odd people assimilate with 1,250 males?" He accused the government of "trying to rush this whole plan through." An Oxfordshire County Council official told the BBC the plan risked making the village and the facility a "lightning rod" for potentially violent far-right protests. The vote attracted the attention of self-styled anti-migration "influencers" online. MoD Bicester (Site A) exists, is disused, and has inbuilt security facilities — but it is also a remote rural facility that is not in easy reach of major built-up areas [FILE: September 8, 2026] Image: Hannah McKay/REUTERS How did the government react? The Labour government has been trying to move asylum seekers housed in hotels, an unpopular legacy they inherited from previous British governments, into disused military facilities by 2029. This follows repeated protests at or near hotels and rented accommodation used for the purpose. Prime Minister Andy Burnham , who only recently took over the rapidly rotating top job in British politics, promised to "look at the issues raised by the community and in the referendum." But he also said that the "vast majority" of British people backed a government plan to stop housing asylum seekers in hotels and argued that it was "fair" to locate holding centers around the country. Speaking to the BBC, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said a former military base was "a better option for housing asylum seekers" than hotels or rented accommodation. One drawback with disused military bases, however, is that they are often intentionally placed in remote and rural areas. This can be ideal for military training and activity, but is less obviously suited to housing migrants with limited mobility and resources. Migration and asylum have been contentious political issues in the UK for decades. But successive governments have faced particular pressure in recent years, with the populist right-wing Reform UK and Restore Britain parties gaining ground against the established political giants the Conservatives and Labour. The most recent manifestation of this was anti-migrant protests in the coastal city of Portsmouth earlier this month . Burnham promises a new political and economic model To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video What does the government say about its plans for MoD Bicester? In a Q+A published in July about its plans for Ministry of Defense (MoD) Bicester (Site A), the British government said the site "would provide basic, safe accommodation and would be designed to be largely self‑sufficient to minimize any impact on the local community." It stressed the plan was still subject to feasibility studies, planning permission requirements and other red tape. It didn't state how many people would be housed there, except to say: "The Home Office would take a phased approach to full occupancy, starting with smaller numbers at first." It did specify that the facility would hold males aged 18-65. The government said that if used, the site would be in operation for a minimum of 10 years. Relocating to military bases was "just the first step in the government’s work to exit hotels and source more appropriate accommodation to meet our statutory obligations," it said. Safety for the local community, staff, and those accommodated on site would be "of the utmost importance," it said. The facility would be monitored round the clock by a security provider and via surveillance footage. It would also be "designed to be as self-sufficient as possible including laundry facilities and communal spaces," the British government said. https://www.politico.eu/article/melencho.text: PARIS — French far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon is betting his blunt style and socially radical agenda will convince first-time voters to back him en masse and propel him into a runoff duel against far-right front-runner Marine Le Pen in 2027. After embracing similar tactics in regional elections earlier this year , Mélenchon has increasingly set himself up on the campaign trail as a foil to the anti-immigration Le Pen by embracing a vision of what he calls “a new France” that celebrates diversity rooted in immigration. The position makes him an outlier domestically — most French politicians believe the Republic should be colorblind — and in much of Europe, where leaders across the political spectrum have tried to project toughness on migration to contain the rise of nationalist forces like Le Pen’s National Rally. Mélenchon’s opponents also accuse him of playing identity politics and openly courting minority voters, Muslims in particular. Advertisement Advertisement But polls show the plan is working at the moment. A survey conducted by Cluster17 exclusively for POLITICO last week had Mélenchon tied for second place with center-right candidate Edouard Philippe at 19%. And a Harris Interactive poll released Monday showed the pugnacious former teacher at 18% — against 16% for Philippe. Le Pen remained well ahead of the pack in both surveys, receiving more than 30% of the vote. The Cluster17 poll showed 47% of respondents younger than 35 backed Mélenchon. That’s more than twice the 22% that Le Pen, who placed second among that demographic, was seen receiving. Strategists from Mélenchon’s party, France Unbowed, told POLITICO that they believe young voters, working-class citizens and those with immigrant roots will be motivated to head to the polls for the first time to back their champion given his platform. Mélenchon is the only leading candidate accusing the French state of pushing systemic racism and Islamophobia and denouncing police brutality. He is Israel’s most vocal critic on the French political stage. And he has promised ambitious policies to tackle climate change, including shifting towards 100% renewable energy. Road to the second round France Unbowed points to the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis — a former home of French royalty, now one of the capital region’s poorest suburbs and home to a large working-class population, many of them of immigrant descent — as potential proof of concept. Advertisement Advertisement Mélenchon won nearly 50% of the vote in the first round of the 2022 presidential election in the district that includes the Paris suburb of Saint-Denis. Turnout was 61.2%, whereas the national average was 73.7%. And France Unbowed scored its biggest-ever victory there when its candidate, Bally Bagayoko, scored a decisive victory in local elections earlier this year, netting more than 50% of the vote in the first round and negating the need for a runoff. But Mélenchon remains a divisive figure. Seventy-three percent of those polled by Cluster17 earlier this month said there was little to no chance they would ever vote for the France Unbowed leader. Only 62% felt the same way about Le Pen. Marine Le Pen speaks in the National Assembly in Paris on Dec. 4, 2024. | Alain Jocard/AFP via Getty Images “France Unbowed has built a strong, cross-class core,” said a parliamentarian for the rival center-left Socialist Party, who was granted anonymity to discuss his opponents’ campaign. “But enlarging their base seems very difficult.” As things stand, Mélenchon’s strategy of zooming in on voters who are most likely to vote for him appears to be tracing a path towards the runoff. On the flip side, polling indicates that he would lose by a significant margin against Le Pen in a second round — though pollsters and political scientists urge caution when it comes to polling a runoff so early in a campaign. “You need to take things one step at a time. Running a runoff campaign before the first round is a grave mistake that has cost several favorites their election in the past,” said Antoine Léaument, a France Unbowed lawmaker and strategist. Immigration and asylum Oxfordshire villagers to launch legal fight against asylum centre plan Parish council of Piddington, which symbolically voted to leave UK over plan, says it will ‘absolutely’ take legal action UK politics – live updates Rajeev Syal Home affairs correspondent Fri 13 Nov 2026 05.47 EST Last modified on Fri 13 Nov 2026 06.26 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Ministers will face a legal challenge over plans to convert a Ministry of Defence site near the Oxfordshire village of Piddington into accommodation for more than 1,200 detained asylum seekers. It emerged on Thursday that Angela Rayner, the housing and communities secretary, had approved full planning permission , a decision welcomed by the Home Office, who want to end the use of asylum hotels. Tim McNally, the local parish council chair, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme there would be “many actions” by villagers, and that ministers should “absolutely” be braced for a legal challenge, which would need to be lodged within the next six weeks. Ministers have faced opposition over the plans from villagers, who even made a symbolic attempt to declare the village independent from the rest of the country after a referendum of its 350 residents. Asked how the village would respond, McNally said: “There’s going to be many actions, you will see. We will disclose that as we move forward.” Asked if ministers should be braced for a legal challenge, he said: “Absolutely, absolutely.” View image in fullscreen The vacant Ministry of Defence site where the proposed asylum centre may be built. Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty Images Campaigners could also apply the new Hillsborough law, which is being considered by parliament. Once passed, the law would create a legally enforceable duty of candour that compels public officials and authorities to act transparently when investigations and inquiries take place. “Today is a day of reflection, and we’ll work out where we plan to go from this point. But I will say, the Hillsborough law is there for a reason, and we’re going to apply it,” he said. Luke Pollard, a defence minister, said the government would continue to engage with the community. He told LBC: “It’s pretty obvious that there’s a strong sense of feeling from the community around Bicester, especially in Piddington. “The Home Office continues to engage with those. There’s still a few more stages to go here, so it’s not yet fully locked in and delivered, so that we can understand where the concerns are, so they can be mitigated.” A Home Office spokesperson said a final decision to proceed had yet to be taken. “The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election. “This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community.” Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative party leader, said the plans were a “betrayal of the women of Piddington” and “emblematic of Labour and Angela Rayner’s disregard for the law and women and girls’ safety”. She said on social media: “When I visited Piddington I met a village terrified of what was about to land on their doorstep. The government said it was listening, instead it’s completely ignored this community’s concerns. “The 1,000+ male migrants that Labour are about to deposit in Oxfordshire are in Britain illegally. They should be deported as soon as possible.” Explore more on these topics Immigration and asylum Oxfordshire Local politics England news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Angela Rayner grants planning approval for asylum centre in Piddington despite local opposition ‘I feel free now’: Shabana Mahmood’s immigration shake-up provokes mixed emotions Court rules against Home Office in asylum seeker kidnapping case Mahmood’s migration changes may harm women and children, Labour MP warns UNHCR criticises UK’s 30-year ‘earned settlement’ plans for refugees UK to deploy facial recognition in biggest-ever immigration crackdown How will UK immigration rules change under Shabana Mahmood’s latest plans? Sentinel photo by Dan DeLoach Zachery Stowell Photo submitted by Oneida County Sheriff Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save CLAYVILLE — Evidence of possible drug use was discovered after a 23-year-old man was taken into custody on accusations of attacking two co-workers with a hatchet at Pratt & Whitney on Friday, Nov. 6, according to an application for a temporary extreme risk protection order from the Oneida County Sheriff’s Office. The temporary order was granted by a judge on Tuesday, Nov. 10. A hearing is scheduled for next week. Several reports from employees and sheriff’s deputies were filed alongside the application. The reports provided further details on the response to the attack, including the accused attacker saying “things that did not make sense” and evidence of drug use found in his vehicle. Authorities said Zachery Stowell, 23, of Poland, attacked security guard Moulay Amrani and employee Nicholas Sutton at HMI Metal Powders Pratt & Whitney on Main Street in Clayville at around 4:30 p.m. Friday, Nov. 6. Authorities said Stowell used a hatchet to attack both men, striking them both multiple times in the head. Stowell was also an employee. Amrani remained hospitalized in critical condition as of Tuesday morning, authorities stated. Sutton was treated and released. Victim statement Sutton gave a statement to investigators. He said he first encountered Stowell in the lobby when Stowell was trying to get into the building, and Sutton worked to verify his employment status to let him in. Later that day, Sutton said he got a call over the radio that Stowell was back trying to get in, so Sutton started making his way to the lobby. “I then observed an individual whom I knew to be Zachery jogging towards me. When Zachery was about 15-20 feet away from me he stated something along the lines of ‘I’m sorry Nick’ or ‘I’m sorry I have to do this Nick’,” Sutton told investigators. “I then observed Zachery cock his right arm back and I saw his arm come forward. I then put my arms up to block the blow, but he still hit me on the top of my head. I was in shock and he then struck me in the area of my chest, causing me to lose my balance, falling backwards.” Sutton described the fight and getting struck in the side of the head with the hatchet. He told investigators how he fought back and got control of the hatchet while they fought on the ground. He said other employees showed up quickly and pulled Stowell off of him. “Zachery made a comment saying ‘I already killed somebody,’ and then said something along the lines of please let me go,” Sutton described. “Zachery then said out loud just shoot me.” Employee statements Multiple law enforcement officers with the Sheriff’s Office and state police responded to Pratt & Whitney. These officers took witness statements from employees on the scene. One employee told investigators that Stowell approached him outside the building before the attack. “The male seemed off and was very jittery and mumbling his words,” the employee told investigators. The employee said Stowell asked if the employee could let Stowell into the building, but the employee repeatedly denied him. The employee said Stowell had a “black in color object coming out of the male’s sleeve on his left arm.” Authorities said Stowell attacked Amrani first at the guard station in the lobby, then went outside and encountered Sutton. Authorities said Sutton was able to fight back and gain control of the hatchet. Several employees responded to Sutton’s cries for help and they pulled Stowell off and pinned him to the ground, authorities stated. “Nick continued to yell for help as I approached while the other male tried to get the hatchet back from Nick. I then ran over and stepped on the hands of the other guy to prevent him from getting the hatchet back,” one employee told investigators. “Both Nick and the other guy let go of the hatchet. I was able to pick up and throw the hatchet about 30-40 feet away. After getting the hatchet away from the suspect several other employees at Pratt Whitney subdued the suspect by grabbing his arms and legs and pinning him to the ground.” One employee described finding Amrani still in his chair with severe injuries, which he tried to put pressure on. The employee said Amrani was not moving or talking, that “the only movement he had gotten out of him was when he had turned his eyes towards him.” An employee with EMT training took over care of Amrani at one point, and other employees assisted him until rescue personnel arrived. Drug evidence Once Stowell was in custody, one deputy reported that he dragged a “passively resisting” Stowell to a patrol car and sat him down. “The male was talking about things that did not make sense and was acting lethargic. In my training and experience, he was acting like someone who was under the influence of narcotics,” the deputy reported. Stowell told the deputy that he took “two live ones,” the report stated, which the deputy later learned meant “Speed Balls,” a mixture of cocaine and heroin. One officer said Stowell was also speaking about “religious figures.” Several officers took an inventory of Stowell’s motor vehicle. In their reports, they said they found empty plastic baggy corners with white residue, a straw with white residue, two $1 bills with white residue, multiple bags of clothes and trash scattered about. Past incident One employee said she had been speaking with Stowell for several months because Stowell was being mandated to seek help from an Employee Assistance Program due to another incident at the workplace where he “had not been acting normally during one of his shifts in early August.” She said Stowell was referred to the program on Aug. 20. The employee said Stowell normally worked the 2 p.m. to midnight shift from Monday to Thursday and had not been scheduled to work on the day of the attack. The employee told investigators that Stowell spoke to her on Nov. 4 regarding Family and Medical Leave Act paperwork. “While he was in my office, he appeared to be sad like he was going through something with his home life,” the employee told investigators. “He didn’t make any strange statements at this time. He did not appear that he was sad to the point where he was going to harm himself or others. He then left my office without incident.” Stowell is scheduled for a felony hearing in Paris Town Court on Friday afternoon, Nov. 13. Stowell is charged with two counts each of second-degree attempted murder, second-degree assault and fourth-degree possession of a weapon, as well as one count each of third-degree assault and resisting arrest. He is being held in lieu of bail in the county jail.
